Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) as to what steps have been taken to ensure the movement of coal from Alberta to Ontario. Last session a sum of money was made available for the purpose of ascertaining the exact cost per ton of transporting coal from the west to the east and to meet any deficit that might arise by reason of the transportation costs being greater than $7 per ton. Large quantities of coal are now obtainable, in fact I am advised that 100,000 tons could be supplied in three weeks if that quantity could be used in central Canada. I understand that the National Railway management did not avail itself of the $25,000 subvention voted by parliament. If a rate of $7 per ton could be assured for future shipments beyond the 25,000 tons that has been or is about to be moved, and that has not absorbed any part of that subvention, there would be a ready market

Chicago Drainage Canal

for large quantities of coal in central Canada. If the hon. minister has any observations to make they will be gratefully received by those who are actively interested in coal production in Alberta.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite correct .that last year parliament voted $25,000 for the specific purpose of moving a quantity of coal from Alberta to Ontario, which movement was to be of the nature of a test. A careful accounting of the transportation costs was to be kept by a nominee of the Alberta government. Arrangements were all completed, as I understood the matter both from Sir Henry Thornton and Premier Greenfield, and the government of Canada was to contribute $1 a ton if the rate should be $8; if it should be $9, the Alberta government was to contribute the other dollar, making $2 in all. However, just before the inception of the movement the railway company handled the 25,000 tons without calling upon either government to make good any loss that might accrue. Therefore that money has not been used for the purpose for which it was voted.
About six weeks ago, when it began to become apparent that the strike in the anthracite field might create a fuel shortage in the central portion of Canada, or what we call the fuel area, the fuel board took steps to ascertain the situation. We found at that time that seventy per cent of the quantity required for this area had been already moved into the country. Since that time I cannot say definitely what further quantity has come in. We took occasion to notify the railway companies that if they were required to do so we would be greatly obliged if they would mobilize their rolling stock at convenient points to hurriedly move large quantities of coal to central Canada both from the east and the west. So far no serious situation has developed, largely I think owing to the very mild weather that we have been experiencing; but should the situation become acute we are ready to lend every assistance we can, and I know that the railway companies are prepared to move the coal very rapidly if a market can be found for it. Of course, it will mean that the prices will be somewhat higher, but in view of the possibility of a shortage it will be necessary to take every precaution to meet any emergency. [DOT]

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the House takes up the Orders of the Day, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) if the government would be willing to lay on the table of the House-previous to taking up the usual business after the Address is carried or not-the correspondence passed between the Canadian government and the British government with reference to the Locarno treaty, the preliminary negotiations, the concluding of the treaty itself and any part thereof which may have been the subject of an exchange of views between the two governments after the treaty, especially in regard to the possible adherence of Canada and the other dominions to the .treaty, by virtue of Article 9. It seems to me of the utmost importance, before the House broaches the subject, that the members -and senators-be furnished with all the documents of this international debate, the consequences of which may be very serious for the world in general and for the dominions in particular, in order to allow both Houses to enlighten themselves on the data of the problem. I would respectfully ask the government to kindly bring down said correspondence at their earliest convenience.

Mr. Speaker, there was in fact, correspondence exchanged between the Canadian government and the Imperial government with reference to the Locarno treaty. However, I must inform my hon. friend that so far as we are concerned, we have no objection to it being made public. the day, in order that members may have the opportunity of studying this question, perhaps during the week end, I shall lay this document on the table of the House, moreover, the distribution office will have copies for all the members.

The government has had the Locarno treaty printed, with the various arbitration conventions relating to it-not only the treaty between Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Belgium, but also the treaty between France and Poland and that between France and Czecho-Slovakia. I will lay a copy of that document on the table a little later to-day, if the House will allow me, and there will be copies in the distribution office for rhe use of those members who desire to study this matter over the week-end.

The House resumed from Thursday, January 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. C. Elliott for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer a few remarks on the subject matter contained in the Speech from the Throne, and also on some of the speeches that have been delivered in this debate. I do not think that I should offer any apology if I make these remarks in English. It has been a matter of discussion and controversy in recent years whether we French-Canadians, when we speak in this House, should use our own mother tongue, and thereby preserve the traditions of bilingualism, which are characteristic of this parliament. I admit at once that much can be said in favour of such a practice, and I
3*2
The Address-Mr. Rinfret

fee! sure that when the occasion arises, there will always be on this side, and perhaps even on the other side of the House, speakers who will avail themselves of their privilege of using their maternal tongue, ithe French language; but in other cases it may seem perfectly obvious, and even imperative, that if we wish to convey our ideas and our thoughts to members on all sides of the House, or to reply to some of the remarks that have been made from other quarters of the House, we should employ a language that will convey our thoughts to every member. We do not experience any comfort in doing that. Cn the contrary we realize that we labour under quite a handicap in using a language not as familiar to us as our own maternal tongue. At the same time, as I have already said, we have to do this because we are anxious to establish a medium of communication, a corridor as my right hon, friend (Mr. Meighen) would say, between our minds and the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. And if I wanted to rely on an example, coming from a sturdy champion of the French language, 1 could point out to certain papers, which have discussed the matter in the past, that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) himself, when he rose in this House a few days ago after addressing to you, Mr. Speaker, a few complimentary remarks in French-to which I desire to add an expression of my personal regard and admiration-proceeded in beautiful English to discuss the question then before the House. It is in the same spirit and influenced by the same motive, that I wish to-day to discuss the Speech from the Throne and some of the speeches that have been uttered by hon. members, in the English language. Perhaps I may be permitted to crave the indulgence of the House if I find it a little harder to do so in the English tongue, if I have not as great facility in giving expression to my sentiments as I would if I were speaking French.
First of all I desire to add my compliments to those which have already been paid to the mover and seconder of the Address. The mover of the Address (Mr. Elliott) gave us a picture of financial conditions as we find them to-day in the Dominion, a picture far different from the one drawn for us during the recent electoral compaign in the columns of Tory newspapers and in the speeches of Tory orators. Yet, my hon. friend made that picture very convincing. He produced figures, he produced statistics, which demonstrate beyond a shadow of doubt that this country is at least much more prosperous than the Conservative party were willing to give the 
Liberal government credit for during the last campaign. As for the seconder of the Address, my good friend the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe), I understand he was selected for that honour because he is the youngest member of the House, and upon that I also almost compliment him. There is perhaps some melancholy in the fact that we members who have only been in this House a few years are already called upon to compliment other members upon their youth. But I do wish to remind the hon. member that youth while a precious thing is bound to disappear with the passage of the years. The hon. member made a fine speech, notable in delivery and elegant both in thought and in style, and I am sure he will be a distinguished acquisition to the debating strength of the House.
I also wish to welcome hon. members of both sides who are in the present parliament and whom we all like to see with us. I need not add that my welcome is a little more spontaneous when it is directed to hon. gentlemen on this side, but if I forget for one moment the party spirit with which I am imbued, it is in all sincerity that I welcome hon. members generally.
Previous to the present discussion we had a very interesting debate, the first of the session. We discussed whether this government had done right in summoning parliament, and in presenting the Speech from the Throne. The discussion was most interesting to a layman as I profess to be. We listened to precedents being quoted and cited on both sides of the House, and we were highly interested indeed in being told what took place fifty, a hundred, years ago and even farther back in the history both of this country and of England. For my part, I think that we should not attach too much importance to precedents. After all, Mr. Speaker, what is a precedent if not merely a solution that has been applied in the past to some new situation. There is no precedent that was not an innovation in its day; and if we are much interested in being told what took place under James I. George II, or Henry V, who have all been dead a long time, nevertheless, for my part, I rejoice that we have been able to proclaim the paramount power of this parliament; and representing as we do, not the dead monarchs or statesmen of a century ago, but the living Canadian people of to-day, that we have reached a proper decision, that we have come to the conclusion that we have full authority to deal to-day with the current affairs of the country. A division took place, and I remember that when the vote was

The Address-Mr. Rinfret
counted, hon. gentlemen opposite could not refrain from demonstrations of enthusiasm at the wonderful success they had achieved. These enthusiastic demonstrations were in marked and distinct contrast to the comments we read in the newspapers next day.
With respect to that vote, I wish to emphasize this particular feature of it. It was but natural that the Liberal members of the House should support the government. It was quite natural, also, that the Conservative members should support the amendment even if they did not like it. But we have here- counting the votes of members of the Progressive, Labour, and Independent parties twenty-eight independent members and out of those twenty-eight independent voters the government was able to command not less than twenty-three, a very large proportion of the independent vote in this House and, may I not add. a very large proportion of the independent vote throughout the country. Viewed from that angle, Mr. Speaker, you will discover that although the government only secured a majority of three on the first vote-a majority I am sure that will increase with the coming divisions of the session-it was at least able to command practically four-fifths of the independent vote in this chamber, and also of the independent vote in the country.
The opposition laid much stress on the fact that they were the largest group and that they could command the largest popular vote out of the groups in this House. I should like, however, to point out a fact which has been already indicated but not quite fully. That is that a certain number of hon. gentlemen opposite, although they have been elected in the counties they represent, do not hold a majority of the votes cast in those counties.
I have not the full list in my hand, I have not been able to secure the information from the Chief Electoral Officer, but from reports published time after time in the newspapers we find out that in a certain number of counties, especially in the western provinces, hon. gentlemen opposite, although they were elected, and although they were entitled to their election under our electoral system, at the same time did not poll the majority of votes in their respective constituencies. That is true, for instance, in the electoral district of Neepewa where the Conservative member (Mr. Murphy) polled 3,461 votes; the Progressive, 3,332 and the Liberal 1,809. So that 5,000 votes were cast against the hon. member whereas he himself only polled 3,400. That is also true of the division of East Calgary, where the Conservatives polled 5,562 votes, and the combined vote of the Labour and Liberal candidates amounted
to over 6,000. That is true of the constituency of East Edmonton, where the Conservatives .polled 3,927 votes, the Liberals 3,440, and the Labour man 2.765, or a majority against the member now sitting in this House of pretty nearly 6,000. That is true also of the constituency of Marquette. You heard from that county the other night. The hon. member (Mr. Mullins) spoke on behalf of 4,219 electors who voted for him, but we find that the Progressive candidate polled 4,084 votes and the Liberal 1,665 votes-there being a majority of almost 1,600 votes against the hon. member. That is also true of the constituency of Springfield, Manitoba, where the Conservative candidate obtained 2,268 votes, the Liberal 1,721 and the Progressive 1,660. I will not weary the House with more statistics.
Has the hon. member got the figures for Moose Jaw, Saskatoon and numerous other points in Saskatchewan represented by members on the other side?
He was not looking for those figures.

I have not those figures.
I was merely arguing this point that my right hon. friend claims he has the largest number of seats in this House, and I say that in a number of constituencies his supporters did not poll a majority of the votes. I do not say this did not happen in other places. Out of" 116 seats which the right hon. member obtained, his candidate in a number of cases polled a minority of the votes in the constituency. I know very well that my right hon. friend would want me to make a diSerent speech from the one I am going to make. If he interrupts me fifteen times I will reply to him as graciously as I can, but he will not prevent me from going on.
My hon. friend always stated that the main plank in his platform and in his appeal to the people was his fiscal policy. We have heard speeches from the Conservative members from the west since the commencement of this debate, and Conservative members from the Maritime provinces. They stated very plainly that so far as they were concerned the tariff was not the main issue; it was transportation. We heard the speech of the hon. member for Marquette; he stated that transportation was the whole thing with him. He blamed the Liberal government for not having reduced the transportation rates and for not having been able to put through a measure which would restrain the ocean shipping combine. Far from supporting the policy of my right hon. friend, his argument was that we had not
The Address-Mr. Rinjret

gone far enough. He wants the rates further reduced and he would like this government to try during the course of the session to bring forth a measure to restrict the combines on the seas and to lower the rates on transAtlantic transportation. That was tfhe argument of my hon. friend, and it was as different from the policy of his right hon. leader as from our policy.
In reference to the Maritime provinces, we all know that their problems are very closely connected with the problems of the western' provinces. They are practically in the same situation. The member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) stated that so far as he was concerned he would be in favour of a tariff that would be heightened on certain articles, but lowered on other articles. He was not at all in favour of high protection. He was in favour of a tariff that would cover the various items differently, according to the exigencies of the situation.
Then what was the argument of the hon. member forVictoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming)? Transportation. He wanted the grain from the west to come to St. John, and he prayed to us that we should take measures to reduce the rates on the railways to bring more grain from the west to St. John. We are trying to do that, but are prevented from doing it by the right hon. leader of the opposition. Every time we raised this question in the House the Conservative leader indignantly protested that we should not deal with it. Perhaps counting all these hon. gentlemen from the west or from the Maritime provinces as in favour of high protection on everything, my right hon. friend should be rather thankful if some of the electors, either in the west or in the Maritime provinces, forgot about his own policy. They come here and tell us that they are not cncerned at all with the tariff, but that what they want is merely cheap transportation for their grain or for the products they expect to handle in their harbours en route to their overseas destinations.
When we come to the province of Quebec the question of the popular vote becomes highly interesting. We had an electoral campaign in Quebec, but the Conservative leader never came within the borders of our province, or if he did come it was incognito. He would not let anybody know it, and I am perfectly at liberty to discuss this matter after the statements which have been made, and at the same time to deal with the speech that the hon. member for Kent, N.B., madte yesterday with regard to the election campaign.
Oh, oh.

I will welcome any applause, and I hope when I read some newspaper clippings applause will be forthcoming from the other side. If the hon. member for Kent, N.B. likes newspaper clippings he is going to get more than his share this afternoon. When that hon. member delivered his speech yesterday he even scandalized the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers). When the hon. member for South Winnipeg rose to speak later in the day he could1 not hide his indignation in regard to what had taken place in the province of Quebec. I am sorry my right hon. friend is not in his place. I do not want to be discourteous but it shows what a change has come over the hon. member for South Winnipeg.
My hon. friend has evidently cut off the moustache of his aggressiveness and rather let grow on the back of his head a mane of conciliation which he had not possessed in the past. However, we will deal with these matters in due time.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) did not come to Quebec, but later on when the campaign was over he did favour us with a letter in which he explained why he had not come to that province. This letter from the right hon. gentleman is written to the Hon. Mr. Fauteux, Conservative candidate, dated November 25, 1925, and says:
Canada is a iarge country. I had relatively little ft'ime to cover such an immense territory before polling day. I went to where I was called most insistently.
Before I read any more, let me say that I sincerely sympathize with my right hon. friend in this particular instance, as he will find by my further remarks. He was stating at least the truth in the last sentence that I mentioned :
Canada is a large country.
True Canada is a large country, but the province of Quebec is a very small portion of it. My right hon. friend went to Prince Edward Island and I find no fault with his action in that regard. I have gone there myself on several occasions and it is a very fine little province. But I would think, speaking politically, it might have seemed more important to visit Quebec where there are sixty-five seats than to go to Prince Edward Island where there are only four. Moreover, starting from Ottawa, one cannot go to Prince Edward Island without passing through the province of Quebec. I know my right hon. friend is willing to spend $3,000,000 on the Hudson Bay railway; but surely he never thought of taking that route in order to reach Prince

ber for Kent. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I should now hasten to the last part of my speech. I want to refer to some of the features of the Speech from the Throne. We are not addicted to racial prejudice, notwithstanding what has been said against us, but we will never bow before the prejudice of high protection. We know very well that our friends opposite are too prone to confuse high tariff with protection. There are many ways of protecting industries besides raising the tariff. You may achieve the same purpose if you lower the tariff on raw materials 01 some of the articles entering into the fabrication of the finished goods. You also protect industries most directly if you open to the exports of this country markets in other parts <of the world. That is what the Liberal government has tried to do. It has reduced the tariff on agricultural implements, but it has also reduced the tariff on some of the raw materials entering into the manufacture of these implements. It has increased the British preference on shoes and textiles by 2^ per cent. A much-discussed matter during the last (campaign, was the effect of that decrease on (the shoe industries in Montreal and Quebec. (Much noise was created over the fact that a factory had been closed in St. Hyacinthe. It

The Address-Mr. Rinjret
was said that that was on account of the tariff, but a few months later the Arrow Shoe *.Company of Montreal opened another factory in the same town of St. Hyacinthe, under the isame tariff and the same conditions, and it is [DOT]very prosperous to-day. What are we to conclude from that fact, if not that the tariff alone has not much to do with prosperity or failures-if there are any-in the industrial *world. The government has promised that it will establish a tariff commission.
Will the hon. gentleman say how many industries depending upon the shoe industry have failed and gone out of business?
That would take me pretty far. I am sorry my right hon. friend was not in our province during the campaign, where he would have heard the whole matter discussed1.
Many industries depending on the shoe industry have gone out of business in Ontario.

My hon. friend will readily understand that I cannot open up the whole question of the shoe industry. I must confess that I am flattered at the great desire of these gentlemen to hear me, but I must not forget that other speakers are to follow, and must not prolong my remarks unduly. The reason I mentioned the tariff was merely because I wanted to come to the amendment of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. If I understand the amendment well, the right hon. gentleman finds no fault at all with the Speech from the Throne.
Oh yes.

He is merely adding a paragraph to it, and that paragraph is a most extraordinary one when it comes from a high protectionist like my right hon. friend. In my opinion it is merely a statement of generalities which are intended to indicate a policy without stating it, and if I were in the position of the Progressive members of this House, and had to choose between that amendment and the Speech from the Throne, I would not hesitate for one moment.
The Speech from the Throne this year, Mr. Speaker, is simply the re-embodiment of what has been the Liberal policy in all times, and more especially during the last four years in which the Liberal party has been in power at Ottawa. If our hon. leader and his government have tried to achieve anything, it has been to unite Canada, and more especially to bring the east and the west together. We consider that we cannot govern this country
unless we give close attention to the needs of every province in the Dominion. I am proud to say that in the province of Quebec we have resisted appeals from the high tariff advocates to ally ourselves with them against the interests of the west. Those scrupulous Tories would not dare to discuss war matters of past years, but they would not hesitate one moment to stir up within our own borders a financial and economic war between the east and the west. The victory of the Liberal party in Quebec was not the victory of a prejudice; it was the victory over a prejudice. ' It was the victory of the good common sense of the people of Quebec, imbued with a strong Canadian spirit, that true spirit of confederation which should animate us all and which we should all try to develop and make the ruling Canadian sentiment-a desire for Canadian unity, based on an acknowledgment of the needs and aspirations of all groups of our population.
The Quebec victory was not won on the grounds that have been stated by the hon. member for Kent, N.B. The Quebec victory, and I say it with pride, was a refusal to listen to the big Tory interests in the east which are now bidding for western support because they need it, but who, if they had secured a majority in this House would have had no other idea than that of swamping and crushing western interests. Mr. Speaker, Quebec would not yield to that prejudice. Far from heeding any of the arguments which recalled memories of the war, Quebec refused to listen to the appeals of the Tory party and the Tory candidates in our own province who tried to unite us with the high protectionists of the east against the best interests of the west and against the best interests of the whole country. I say again, the meaning of the Liberal victory in Quebec is the intense desire of Quebec for national unity, for tolerance and justice for all parts of the country, and more especially for the true and just consideration of the needs of the west in this parliament.
Only one word more, Mr. Speaker, and it is to rejoice that in the evolving of the policies of this country parliament and members of parliament are gradually becoming more and more considerate. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) expressed regret that in the last parliament the government had to yield to demands from different groups of the House, and he cited several examples; for instance, that the Minister of National Defence had to reduce his estimates. That was an awful spectacle, he said, because, forsooth, Liberal and Progressive members had put before parliament the desire of their constituents,
The Address-Mr. Rinjret

and the government had listened to them. Of course that could not appeal at all to a Tory mind, but it does appeal to my mind, Mr. Speaker. In the past, some decades ago, we often heard the insinuation that the government of this country was too much influenced from the other side of the ocean; we used to be told that Downing Street was governing Canada. Then we passed to another period when it was said, especially during the war, that we had in this country government by order in council, and that that was not proper. In the last parliament the Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, declared that his government considered itself not as a group of supermen but as a committee of parliament who were willing to listen to and consider the demands of the representatives of the people sitting in this House, and Mr. Speaker, if the present make-up of this House results in more of that spirit, I welcome it. Perhaps we Shall come to a time when we shall say not merely that the policy of this country is not to be decided upon by Downing Street or even in the council chamber in the eastern block in Ottawa, but that it shall be evolved and decided upon in the sole and only chamber proper for that purpose, right here in this House of Commons where the representatives of the Canadian people sit and are convened.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you are not already over-weary of receiving felicitations on your re-election to your high office, I should like to preface what I have to say to this House by paying to you as a distinguished member of a great race, and a representative of one of the oldekt of the constituent parts of this Dominion, my tribute as the representative of one of the ridings of the capital city of one of the youngest provinces of Canada. If my constituents should at any future election so far forget, in a moment of mental aberration, their own good fortune and that of the country, as well as of myself, as not to return me to any future house, one of the most striking, colourful and impressive recollections I should always carry with me would be that of your dignified presidency over this chamber.
I hesitate to assure the House that I will not trespass upon its time for undue length, because what is "undue length" is undoubtedly a matter of opinion, and I have observed that it appears to be the custom of hon. members upon that question to form their own opinion.
I listened throughout this debate with assiduous care for some effective answer from *hon. members opposite and particularly from

*ministers on the treasury benches, to the criticism and charges levelled by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) against the past and projected policy of the government. I 'have heard none. We did hear from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) certain expressions such as "outrageous misrepresentation" at the very moment when he himself was garbling the language of the right hon. leader of the opposition and grossly misrepresenting his political statements and political position. I do not for one moment assume that the Minister of Agriculture realized what he was doing, because I have no right to sacrifice the honesty of any member on the altar of his intelligence. But whatever be the explanation, reputable or disreputable, the fact remains unaltered that in the very citations which he read from tlhe statements of the right hon. leader of the opposition he himself, immediately afterwards, put them into his own language-language that was almost diametrically opposed to what was actually said. If the ministers who occupy the treasury benches are not too high seated in Olympus for my feeble and very modest congratulations to reach them, I should wish to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Agriculture for the wonderful expert ness, the wonderful dexterity and skill, which they have displayed in this House in setting up and knocking down men of straw; and the thuds which followed the fall of these dummies were hailed with such applause by gentlemen behind the ministers who were operating that I am forced to believe they have never been accustomed on that side of the House to anything better.
During the debate upon the amendment to the motion for consideration of the Speech from the Throne, the Minister o!f the Interior (Mr. Stewart) ventured to assume two roles, that of historian and that of prophet. He assumed the role of an historian when he essayed to tell the members of this House exactly why the Liberal candidate was beaten in Easi Edmonton in the recent election. The Minister of the Interior on the earlier occasion to which I refer, indulged in prophecy. At the conclusion, of the Crimean war that great tribune of the British people, John Bright, made one of the most famous speeches of his life, which, from a phrase that occurred in it, got the name and was immortalized as the "angel of death" speech. After the speech was over, Disraeli said to him that he would give almost anything he had to be able to make a speech like that, and John Bright, with his characteristic candour said: "So you could, if you were an honest man." I refer to this because we recollect that in connection with the budget of 1924 the Minister of the Interior made another speech which will go down to posterity, not as the "angel of death " speech, but as the "death knell" speech. I have already said that to attempt to write history is a dangerous thing. To attempt to indulge in prophecy is, I consider, a still more dangerous thing. If the minister must assume the role of a prophet, I would suggest, humbly and reverently, that he should remember two things: first, to try to select an event so far distant that he will certainly not be there when it does not take place; and second, if he must select an event that is of an impending nature, if he must make a prophecy regarding the death of any policy or movement, to make sure, before he buys the whiskey and candles for the wake, that the corpse is dead, and before his hand grasps the bell rope to ring out the tocsin telling the neighbours that the joyful occasion is on, to make sure that the corpse will not rise out of the coffin to enfold him in its cerements and push him into the box which he had intended for it.
Protection is very far from being dead. Coming from the west, I venture to say that protection is more alive than it has been for a long time. There is a general recognition throughout the country, even throughout the west, that protection is necessary for the welfare of the Dominion as a whole. There is a general recognition of the fact that if we assume, for purposes of argument, that proper and effective protection of industry is not in the interest of agriculture, then there are only two solutions possible if we are to have a national policy, if we are to have a system that is to be of benefit to all sections of the country, east and west, and all types and forms of industry, manufacturing and agriculture. Those two solutions are briefly these: Either in the interest of agriculture to do away with protection altogether and bonus industry, or in the interest of industry to have a sufficient, proper and effective protection and to give agriculture some countervailing
benefit in the form either of concessions in the matter of freight rates or of some protection for agricultural products, or possibly a combination of both forms. That being so, and that being the feeling throughout this country, I am not at all surprised that in the Speech from the Throne there has been an abandonment of at least one of the old tariff shibboleths of the Liberal party.
I refer to the shibboleth which we have so often heard cried from the Liberal camp, the shibboleth of "Tariff for revenue purposes only." That has been jettisoned. You have only to look at the Speech from the Throne to find how true that statement is. This is the policy of the government:
In their view the incidence of this form of taxation should bear as lightly as possible upon the necessaries of life and on agriculture and other primary industries . . . that changes in the tariff should be made only after the fullest examination of their bearing upon both .primary and manufacturing industries, and that representations requesting increase or decrease of duties should be made the subject of the most careful investigation and report by a body possessing the necessary qualifications.
Not even the most purblind protagonist of " Tariff for revenue purposes " could claim that that is such a tariff. It is the enunciation of a doctrine that is at least sane, namely, that you have to consider the tariff not only from the standpoint of what revenue it will produce, but also from the effect it will have upon the industries of the country; that you have so to adjust the incidence and weight of taxation that it shall not merely produce revenue but shall have the best possible consequences and exercise the most beneficial influences upon that which is most important to a new country, namely, its commerce and its trade.
Now, I do not wonder that there has been this growing feeling throughout the country, for the simple reason that everybody at heart is a protectionist-at least with respect to his own product. Labour is protectionist. Labour has secured the position it now occupies, the advantages and powers, the privileges and rights it now possesses, by a programme and policy of protection-primarily by the machinery of protection which it devised, erected and put into operation for itself, and afterwards by the supplementary machinery of protection which quite properly it obtained by parliamentary enactment. I do not think there is a member on this side of the House, or on the other side, who does not from the bottom of his heart hope that Labour will long continue its protective efforts for the purpose of securing to itself every legitimate right, every legitimate advantage, every legiti-

Now, I come to another part of the speech of the mover of the Address in reply with which I am in hearty accord, as I am sure must be all members of the House. That is the part of his speech in which he describes the needs of the Dominion. I am not going to occupy the time of the House by dealing at length with each of them. The first need which he mentions is that of rigid economy. That is a very vague phrase. It may mean anything; it may mean an attitude on economy so rigid that you do not do anything, or it may really be a very serious and strenuous attempt to effect economies in the government of the country. There is a second remedy proposed, that of better markets. I think we all agree with that, but the question which arises in our minds is, what has been done to secure them? What is being done to secure the better markets which we all confess we need? There are two elements in this problem of better markets. One is to keep our own home market as much as possible for our own manufacturers-to extend as far as possible their operations within these markets. The other is to get a larger share of the markets of foreign countries-the United States, for example. What is being done to further either of these two objects? We say that the chief instrument by which both of these necessary ends may be attained by any country is a
proper fiscal policy. We say that we should use the vast natural resources with which divine Providence has endowed this country -our nickel, asbestos and other natural resources and minerals-for the purpose of getting entrance into the markets of the United States. What use are we making of them? I think it was the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) who, speaking last night, dwelt on the enormous sums of money involved in our trade. I am not interested in the bulk amount; I want to know how it is made up. I want to know how much of our export trade is comprised in the exportation of raw material. You may have an enormous trade between this country and the United States and yet that trade may be little else than the feeding of the country upon its own bowels. Now, I can imagine some hon. gentleman saying: Ah, now we are getting at the real point; this gentleman is advocating retaliation. Well, I am advocating retaliation;
I have always believed in it and have never been ashamed of it. I think it is a common sense principle. It is the policy which the republic to our south would adopt in five minutes if it possessed our -resources. We have natural resources which are absolutely essential to certain industries in the United States-industries in which millions of dollars have been invested, and which could not carry on without us-and we make no use of our possession of these resources for the purpose of fiscal bargaining with that country. We should say: "Unless you give us certain concessions we will retaliate against you in the export of our raw materials, or in any other way which may seem best to us." Let me read to you a passage from an authority on political economy:
A non-protecting duty, on the contrary, would in most cases be a source of gam to t'he country imposing it, in so far as throwing part of the weight of its taxes upon other peo-ple is a gain; but it would be a means which it could seldom be advisable to adopt, being so easily counteracted by a precisely similar proceeding on the other side.
That is, by retaliation.
If England, in the case already supposed, sought to obtain for herself more than her natural share of the advantage of the trade with Germany, by imposing a duty on linen, Germany would only have to impose a duty upon cloth, sufficient to diminish the demand for that article about as much as the demand for linen had been diminished in England by the tax.
That is retaliation.
Things would then be as before, and each country would pay its own tax. Unless, indeed, the sum of the two duties exceeded the entire advantage of the trade; for in that case the trade, and its advantage, would cease entirely. There would be no advantage, therefore, in imposing duties of this kind, with a view to gain by them in the manner which has been

And this is the part I wish lion, members to observe:
-that considerations of reciprocity, which are quite unessential when the matter in debate is a protecting duty are of material importance when the repeal of duties of this other description is discussed. Where does that come from? Some Birmingham authority on political economy of the Chamberlain school? No, but from the political economist of the Manchester school, John Stuart Mill. If I believe in retaliation, I have at least his authority behind me. But I want to go-as 'hon. members opposite may deem it-higher in the scale of authority. Not merely does John Stuart Mill teach this doctrine of retaliation, but the leader of the government himself teaches it. Here is what he said in a speech at Alexandria, Ontario, on the 14th of September. Speaking of the suggestion of a tariff on farm products, Mr. Mackenzie King said:
Suppose a duty were put on fresh fruits and vegetables coming in from the United States; what would the United States do?
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the United States would do what we do, they would do nothing. But the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King knows the United States too well to think they would do nothing. He knows the United States too well not to know that they would retaliate at once, and so he says:
What would the United States do? Would the United States not say, if you put a tariff on our fruits and vegetables, we will put one on yours?
Surely they would. And if that is good policy and sound business for the United States, why is it not good policy and sound business for this country? And so, on the authority of John Stuart Mill and the Right Hon. Mr Mackenzie King, I avow myself an out-and-out retaliationist until by retaliation, if need be, the products of the industries of Canada find a fairer share in the markets of the United States.

Another remedy which the mover of the Address mentioned was more people. With that, too I am in hearty accord. More people, yes; but what have you done to get them? There are three elements in this problem:	The first is the element of keeping on the land the people you already have there; the second is the element of bringing back to the land the people who were on it but who have left; and the third is the element of bringing in new people who were never here before. In my opinion I have given these elements in the order of their importance. The most important problem this government can grapple with is that of keeping on the land the people who are on it now, and the next most important is that of getting back our own people, who know Canada, who have Canadian traditions and Canadian connections, Canadian ties and Canadian viewpoints, rather than bringing new people in. I would much rather have our own people brought back to the land than newcomers brought in. The third element is the least important of all, except for its size; that is all.
In relation to these three problems there are three forces operating. There is the British government across the Atlantic, pouring [DOT] out millions of pounds, for the purpose of what? Of solving the third of these problems, of giving us new people who never were here before. The transportation companies are also willing to pour out millions of dollars to help solve that same problem. They are not particularly interested in keeping people on the land, because the more people move off the land, the more people and the more settlers' effects they will be carrying The third power that is trying to solve this problem is the Canadian government. It is
