Here is the other side of the picture:
"I can tell you as Prime Minister that every time the government was face to face with some western problem, we had to face the false charge that we were acting as we were because we were living in the grace of the Progressives or because we wanted their support-which made it very difficult for us to do many of the things we would have liked to do."
I ask hon. members to consider this: If that was the position of things from 1921 to 1925, if that was the state of affairs when they had a majority over all, if at that time Mr. King was handicapped and hamstrung, hampered, cribbed, cabined and confined by the fact that he was so nearly dependent then on the Progressives vote to keep him in power that he could not bring in any measures he wanted to bring in for fear of a false charge against him of pandering to them, how in the name of common sense is he any better off now? If that statement is true there is only one conclusion to draw from it, and that is that if hon. gentlemen to my left got nothing in the last parliament they will get less in this; if they were chastised with whips in the last parliament they will be chastised with scorpions during this parliament. Either the statement is true or it
The Address-Mr. Bury

is false, and if it is false there is only one conclusion to come to: that is, that we have a Prime Minister in Canada who has so forgotten the dignity of his position and the traditions of constitutional government as to make a false statement for the purpose of party gain, that he may win seats for his own party.
I will only trespass further upon the consideration of the House in order to relate a short story. A negro had been sent up to mend a roof that was very steep-it was a shingled roof which he had been sent up to shingle. In the process of his work he slipped, and as he was falling down the very steep roof he cried out in terror "0 Lawd save this nigger; O Lawd, save this nig-" there his prayer suddenly stopped with, "Never mind Lawd, I done cotch on a nail." Ever since 1924 the Prime Minister of Canada has been slipping. During this process, and especially during the election campaign, he made the most undignified attempts to hold on and thus avoid a disastrous fall, until last week, when he "done cotch on a nail". ,1 hardly think it is worthy to be dignified as a nail, that half-hearted majority of three. It is but a tack. How long that fortuitous and precarious tack will hold I do not know; but when it does give;, the fall of the right hon. gentleman will not be the dignified descent which we would fain see accomplished by the head of the government of this country.

Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate you on the high honour that you have received for the second time? I should also like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Elliott) and the seconder (Mr. Lacombe) of the Address on the splendid way in which they performed their duty. It is said that thought, discussion and the free exchange of ideas ought to bring truth from its deep concealment, and that may be so. But as several excellent addresses have been given in this debate already, and as the discussion is likely to last for several days yet, my contribution will be very brief, and I will try to look to the future instead of to the past.
In 1921 no Liberals were elected in the province of Alberta. Nevertheless the Prime Minister of Canada saw fit to call the exPremier of Alberta to the council table at Ottawa. As there was no vacancy in any constituency in Alberta the people of Quebec graciously allowed that gentleman to represent a constituency in that great province. This, Sir, was an act of courtesy on the part of the electors of Argenteuil and the people of Quebec that was very much appreciated by

the people of Alberta, because it has given them cabinet representation during the intervening years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I will not take up the time of the House telling how I managed to-get elected in the west. Suffice- it to say that I succeeded in - getting !by in some way, and I believe I was as much surprised at the result as the other electors of that constituency. The hon. gentleman who has just preceded me (Mr. Bury) is the member for East Edmonton. All who have listened to his eloquent address will recognize that the hon. member is qualified as an orator. In the early part of his speech, recalling his association with the Minister of fhe Interior (Mr. Stewart) he told us that he had two other qualifications: in the first place he was an honest man, and secondly he was a lawyer. Now, Sir, I do not feel qualified to follow the eloquent gentleman. I have neither the first qualification, nor the third; and if I rightly interpreted the trend of his remarks he believes that none of us on this side of the House have what he considers the second qualification, because he intimates quite seriously that we depend upon Providence for any success which we may have. He mentioned, perhaps inadvertently, that the railways were not sorry to see settlers moving out of this country because they got the business of transporting their effects. I think he hardly meant that, because the railways have been great agents in the colonization of western Canada, and I believe that at present they are acting in conjunction with the government in endeavouring to bring about a real immigration policy which will be of great benefit to the west. Unquestionably the railway companies have been the great agents in the colonization of western Canada, and I believe at the present time they are acting together, in conjunction with the government, to bring about a real immigration policy which will benefit the west.
My hon. friend has no hope that good legislation will result from the present condition of affairs in the House. On that point again I must differ from him, because I believe we are in a position at the present time to get really constructive legislation for this Dominion. Canada is a country producing wheat, coarser grains and live stock, and we produce much more of the products of many of our industries than the local market can consume, or that we can hope it will consume, for many years to come. We are in a very different position here from the people of the United States. That great country has a population of 110,000,000 people. It has a

The Address-Mr. Gershaw
varied climate and varied products and resources. You get the grain and the cattle from the north, the cotton in the south, the tropical fruits in California and in Florida. That country is prosperous because it has free exchange of products within its own borders; so that we cannot mould our policy on the policy which has brought success to the United States. I believe the majority of the people in western Canada favour a lower rather than a higher tariff. Why have they that preference? It is not because they have any quarrel with the manufacturers or the industries of Canada. They are anxious to see the industries prosper, but they have that notion because they believe that any increase in tariff on an article is followed by an enhancement of the price which they must pay for that article. If some assurance could be given them that increased prices would not follow the raising of the duties, I believe they would willingly consent to an increased tariff. The people of western Canada are essentially loyal and patriotic. They have no wish to see the work of confederation undone. The men and the women in the rural parts of that country are a thinking people, a well-informed people on subjects of economy, and they are looking for a higher type of service from public men and more in the way of accomplishments from the government than they have received in the past. The people of foreign origin who have settled amongst us also are patriotic. Largely owing to the influence of the schools, and to the praiseworthy efforts of the young men and women who are engaged 9 p.m. in teaching in the schools, they have come to look upon Canada as the land of their adoption, and you will hear an audience which can hardly grasp the English language sing the national anthem in a way which would make some of us native-born Canadians ashamed of our national pride. I have no hesitation in saying that when the work of racial fusion or racial assimilation is completed, the result will be worthy of our traditions and will show the innate strength and lasting power of British institutions and British civilization. It is not for me to relate the suffering and the want and hardship which I have seen in my work as a medical doctor. But I realize that the purchasing power of the people at this time is extremely low, and I am convinced that what Canada needs just now is legislation in the interests of those who are carrying the heaviest burden.
A large part of the country around Medicine Hat formerly belonged to the rancher. Unfortunately it was thrown open for homesteads some years ago by the then officers of
the federal government. Two good years followed, and a great number of farmers settled there. Then a long series of dry years set in. In addition to the drought, soil drifting, cut-worms and grasshoppers took their heavy toll, so that most of the fanners lost everything they had, including years of hard labour by themselves and their families. They received aid from the federal government, and in view of the misfortunes that have befallen them, misfortune that has come through no fault of their own, I hope the department will be lenient in collecting the claims arising out of the aid so given.
The historic city of Mediciqe Hat is noted not only for its beauty but also as being the centre of the largest field of natural gas in the world. The tourist, after travelling over dry, burnt out country, is glad to see the green trees and the beautiful flowers growing there in such profusion. Not one stick of wood, not one pound of coal is used for heating purposes in that city. Gas is used entirely for heating and largely for lighting. It is sold to the consumer for 22 cents a thousand cubic feet, while the cost of gas here in Ottawa is $1.50. Electricity is used to some extent for lighting and is generated by the gas. In addition to the domestic uses, the natural gas, on account of its steady and constant heat, is used in the manufacture of clay products, bricks, sewer pipes, crockery, glass, and other things of that kind, and also in connection with the production of flowers in the large greenhouses located in that city. Gas is found at a depth of about twelve hundred feet. Lately the people in that district have been drilling for oil and hope to produce oil in commercial quantities in the near future. While dredging was being done at a depth of about twenty-four hundred feet a very large stratum of gas was discovered, so that the city is assured of a supply of natural gas for many years. It is the purest of natural gases, being made up almost entirely of methane.
In Medicine Hat three of the great milling companies of Canada have erected large flour mills. These mills are running at about half their capacity, and I should like to urge that the suggestion made by the Canadian Millers' Association receive serious consideration in this House, namely, that measures be taken to provide for the milling of practically all our Canadian wheat in Canadian mills. While the United States impose a duty of 42 cents per bushel on Canadian wheat entering that country for domestic use, Canadian wheat can be milled in bond in the large American mills almost free of duty, on account of
The Address-Mr. Gershaw

the drawback of 99 cents which is allowed. This flour competes with our Canadian flour in the European market. The quantity which is being milled in bond is gradually increasing, the figures being as follows:
Year	Bushels
1922		 6,000,000
1923		 9,000,000
1924		 13,904,837
From this wheat exported and milled in bond in the United States, about three million barrels of flour has been shipped to the European market. During the year there was a demand for fifteen million barrels of. flour, and one-fifth of that, or three million barrels, was milled in the United States. This means a loss to Canadian industries, Canadian railways and Canadian stock men, as they have not the by-products for feeding purposes. I know I may be misunderstood in this particular regard. I am not advocating and I would not advocate anything that would work out to the detriment of a number of our Canadian citizens.
Would the hon. member be in favour of an export duty in that respect on our wheat, to ensure its being milled in Canada?

I am coming to that just in a minute. I believe the millers claim that the imposition of an export duty against the grinding of Canadian wheat in bond would not depress the price which the farmer receives and would not limit the market of Canadian growers. This does not mean that an export duty should be imposed on wheat that is going to any country in the world for domestic purposes. Wheat, being a food product, should move freely. It does not mean that it would handicap our Canadian farmers in their competition with grain growers of the Argentine Republic or Russia or any other wheat-growing country. But it seems to me it is a question which might well be investigated by this parliament ,and there would be many advantages in preventing our Canadian wheat from being milled in bond while passing through another country.
Mr. MoGIiBBON: Would the hon member take the same stand in regard to asbestos, nickel and pulpwood?

I really am not informed on those particular subjects, and I am going over this very carefully because I wish first of all to make clear that I would not be in favour of anything that would be a detriment to a large portion of our population. But anything that would not work against their best interests, anything that would be in the in-

terest of another class of the people of Canada and would also raise the standard and reputation of our Canadian wheat and have it milled and marketed itnder our own trade mark, with advantage to this country should be carefully considered.
The wheat pool in the west is one of the big selling agencies in Canada and its success is a great tribute to the co-operative organization. Its managers and other shippers may feel that they must ship through routes where they get the best rates. If this makes it necessary for wheat to pass through another country, a bond or surety could be given that it would pass through to its destination unground. I would like to quote briefly this extract from a report of the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission which sat under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Turgeon:
At the present time, the duty on Canadian wheatentering the United States-is 42 cents per bushel. On wheat flour, crashed or cracked wheat, and similar wheat products, the duty is $1.04 per hundred pounds. These duties are practically prohibitive, in their effect. They prevent Canadian wheat or wheat products having access to the American domestic market. On the other hand under the provisions governing milling-in-bond and drawbacks, it is quite possible for the American millers to obtain Canadian wheat virtually free of duty to grind for export. Considerable quantities of Canadian wheat are ground in American mills and exported abroad under these conditions. This American flour gound in American mills, but the product of Canadian wheat, enters into competition with the output of the Canadian flour mills. The benefits of manufacture are lost to Canada, while at the same time, the general benefits of reciprocal free trade in wheat and wheat flour do not exist. It was suggested to us that in view of these conditions, an export duty should be levied at the same rate as the American tariff, upon Canadian wheat and wheat products entering the United States. The American tariff having already closed effectively the domestic market to the Canadian farmers, the result of such a levy would be to eliminate the export of American flour ground from Canadian wheat, and to transfer this market to -the Canadian millers. While, as a general thing, export duties are to be deprecated, the exceptional situation that arises in this instance might warrant such an impost.
Representing, as I do, a city having large mills and a country in which a good deal of grain is grown, I believe this is a question which should receive the serious consideration of the members of this House.
The time has come when light automobiles are more of a necessity than- a luxury, and quite a number of people leave this country and go across the border because light cars and gasoline are so much cheaper there than they are here. There they can buy them and give their families the advantage which such a possession brings. I hope that as the duties are reduced the light car will receive early consideration, because I believe it is wise economy to have such a cheap car on the average farm or ranch in this country.

The Address-Mr. Barber
1 am in favour of the motion which is before the House, because the Speech from the Throne forecasts aggressive policies which have received the approval of the mature judgment of experienced legislators. In fact,
I believe its approval has been very general throughout the country. I consider the carrying out of those policies will mean much to western Canada; and if that is the means of bringing some measure of success and prosperity to the west, all Canada will .benefit thereby. What is of advantage to the great, primary, basic industry of Canada must benefit all other industries. I am, therefore, in favour of the motion so ably moved by the hon. member for West Middlesex.

Mr. Speaker, I belong to the long list of newcomers to this House, and I wish to take this opportunity of falling in line with other members in extending to you hearty congratulations on your election to the honourable position which you now occupy.
On my arrival here to take up my parliamentary duties I wag fortunate enough to come in contact with a gentleman who had some forty years' experience of parliamentary life, and he gave me Some excellent advice. As a newcomer he told me for the first session I ought to keep my eyes and ears wide open, be constantly in my seat, and note and study parliamentary procedure; and that if I undertook to say anything I was to be brief and to the point. After listening to the address this afternoon of the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), an address which extended over two hours, I imagine other new members share my opinion that the advice " to be brief and to the point " should apply generally.
Unlike many of my hon. friends who are so ready to impress the fact upon us, I am not a farmer, neither am I a lawyer; I am just an ordinary business man, who has lived in an agricultural community for over twenty-five years. And I think any man after that length of residence who does not become interested in the problems of his community can not be termed a very good citizen. As member foi the Fraser Valley district of British Columbia I am proud to say that I represent the richest district in the province and one of the richest agriculturally in the whole Dominion. True, that district, extending over 100 miles from west to east, and 50 or 60 miles from the international boundary line northward, contains also great timber areas and mineral resources, but to-night I intend to confine my remarks to matters agricultural, and in particular to two very important branches of it- the dairy and poultry industries. The men 14011-24
engaged in these industries are all of the highest type of Canadian citizenship, energetic and of good business judgment. Many of them are returned soldiers. They have built up good farms, and some of the finest dairy herds in Canada. Sir, if you or any other member of this House hadl the privilege of visiting the stock show at the Royal Winter Fair	at	Toronto	last month	you wouldhave noticed there some dairy stock from British Columbia, and you would also have noticed that the grand championship	as	well as	many other	prizes went
to Fraser valley dairy herds. The Dominion experimental farm is located in my riding and has a long line of prize-winning Holsteins. The management of that farm is held in the highest esteem, and the assistance afforded by the institution is appreciated by the local farmers.
It has	been said	of the dairy	industry thatwhile	it	offers no	opportunity	for acquiring
great wealth, yet it does open one of the surest and safest roads to a competency that is to be found in the whole realm of agriculture to the man who is willing to stick to it. Dairying is without doubt one of the most important industries of Canada. It has grown rapidly. The total production for the calendar year 1925 is estimated at $300,060,000- almost one-third greater than the mineral production of which we are so proud. The mineral production for 1924 was $209,583,406, this including everything that comes out of the earth-the precious metals, copper, zinc, nickel, coal, and the oil and gas that my friend spoke of. The dairy production amounts to about two-thirds of the value of the great wheat crop, which this year is estimated to be worth $450,000,000. We are pleased to note that with increased production we have an increase in exports of about 20 per cent over the previous year. At the same time we find an increase in imports. We imported: butter, 99,748 pounds; cheese, 10,274,338 pounds, or a combined value of $2,343,482. Add to this fresh milk, $12,453; caseine, $26,222; condensed milk, $27,076, and we have a total of $2,409,235 worth of dairy products imported into Canada during the calendar year 1925. From the way we are starting off this year it is quite apparent, Sir, that the importations will be still greater.
The first effect of the trade agreement entered into by our friends opposite has been felt. As has been drawn to the attention of this House by my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen), a large shipment of New Zealand butter has already arrived and has resulted in an immediate drop in price of three cents a

The Address-Mr. Barber

pound. According to the figures supplied to me by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the total imports of butter last year, as I have already stated, amounted to 99,748 pounds. Before the first ten days of this year had passed1, und'er the new trade agreement with Australia over 600,000 pounds of butter had been imported. I got in touch with the Customs department this afternoon and ascertained that instead of the 480,000 pounds mentioned by my hon. leader, over 600,000 pounds of butter has1 already been unloaded here. According to press reports yesterday, which I have not yet been able to confirm, another shipment of two million pounds is on the way, if indeed it has not already arrived. We must all admit that at times even small imports will demoralize a market in any particular commodity, but with such immense imports as we are having under the Australian treaty our butter market will be absolutely swamped and the dairy industry ruined. The dairymen of Canada fully realized what would happen as soon as they read the text of the treaty. And the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mir. Motherwell) knew perfectly well what would happen. In confirmation of this I have but to refer to what the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) quoted to the House the other day from Hansard of 1922, page 808, where we find the Minister of Agriculture stated:
New Zealand, on the other hand, has also a favoured climate and a comparatively short stabling season. It puts its butter right off the grass in British Columbia in competition with our winter-made butter, and we have a hard struggle to compete with it.
The hon. gentleman made this observation in 1922 and put the Australian treaty in force on October 9th, 1925. This butter comes in at one cent a pound with a proposed bonus of six cents a pound. The treaty provides that if Canada undertakes to ship to New Zealand or Australia we must meet the tariff of six cents per pound. Canadian farmers cannot live and compete under this handicap.
Now I wish to refer to the egg situation. If you have been following the daily press you will have noticed that we are having trouble in the poultry industry, and I just wish to say a word or two in regard to that situation. Things are very serious, so serious that I notice in a clipping from a Vancouver paper which reached me yesterday that:
Mr. J. A. McCrae, who runs a poultry farm at Central Park called at The Province office to-day and stated that he knows of three men who are killing off stocks, one of them, he says, having already slaughtered 500 head, another 700 and a third 900. The tragedy of it is that the 'birds have just arrived at their period of peak production when they would have

paid for themselves if the price of eggs had been normal. At the price feed is, however, the loss of keeping them is to great, says, Mr. McCrae: "Feed prices" he says, "run to as high as $68 a ton. Recently I was paying $55 a ton, but the grain was so tough it was almost useless to feed it to the chickens, and I had to get a better grade, which cost $68 a ton. Poultrymen are unable to stand this discrepancy between the 'high price of feed and the low price of eggs," he added.
This is a serious situation, as it applies to British Columbia and to all parts of Canada. The hon. Minister of Agriculture gave the mild weather as the reason for this apparent over-production. No doubt so long as the hon. gentleman occupies his present position the mild weather will continue. I was somewhat amused at that statement. The mention of eggs reminds me of a story of our grand old chieftain, Sir John A. Macdonald. Shortly after an election, when his party had been returned to power, he was visiting in Toronto. A good lady of that city came to him and said: "Sir John, since the Conservative party came into power my hens lay more eggs, bigger eggs, and better eggs than they ever laid before." This was given by Sir John as a joke. The hon. Minister of Agriculture in making his statement the other day was apparently quite serious, but I think it was accepted by the House as a joke. I would rather be inclined to give the government full credit for the condition of the industry to-day, and to give his department some credit for the increase in egg production. I understand that something in the neighbourhood of $5,000,000 is expended by his department on agriculture each year, and no doubt a portion of that amount is used to develop and encourage the poultry industry. The poultry population of Canada has increased 180 per cent during the last twenty-five years, until at the present time it is estimated at nearly 50,000,000. What about the production? During the calendar year 1925 Canada produced 225,000,000 dozen eggs. That seems a large number, but if you figure it out you will find that it is less than one egg per person per day. The Minister of Agriculture says that his department is going to join with other associations throughout Canada in a campaign to encourage the eating of eggs. That is an excellent move, but I think the change in the policy of the government to which I shall refer later would be a great deal better.
W'hat about imports? We imported1 into Canada during the same period from the United States 2,577,400 dozen; from China, 79,174 dozen; from Hong Kong, 51,836 dozen; from Japan, 11,430 dozen; and' a few from

The Address-Mr. Barber
other countries, making a total of 2,721,606 dozen eggs imported into Canada. That means that every person in Canada must have consumed about ten foreign eggs every month in addition to our own good Canadian eggs. These eggs enter from the United States under a duty of three cents per dozen, and under the Australian treaty they come in free. The United States poultry industry is protected by a tariff of eight cents per dozen, and Australia and New Zealand have a tariff of eighteen cents per dozen against us. On behalf of the poultrymen of my district I urge the government to give us what everyone considers to be the only remedy-equal protection to that afforded the United States poultry industry, by raising the Canadian tariff to eight cents. I would suggest that they put into force, in addition, what we already have in British Columbia, the Egg Marks Act. That act has worked out very satisfactorily in British Columbia. Foreign eggs placed on sale in Vancouver must bear the stamp of the country of origin. American eggs are stamped "U.S.A."; Chinese eggs are stamped "China"; Japanese eggs are stamped "Japan"; and so on. I say this method has produced successful results in British Columbia and 1 would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he seriously consider its value. This is the situation as it exists.
A serious condition prevails in the dairying and poultry industries of this country and it is the reason I am on my feet to-night. Petitions have come from all parts of my district; appeals were made in this House last session, I believe, but nothing has been done. I have here the copy of a petition forwarded by one of the farmers' institutes of our province. It says that a copy is to be forwarded to the Minister of Agriculture, and no doubt he has received it. The letter accompanying the petition says:
I am enclosing a copy of resolutions passed at the annual meeting of the Surrey Farmers' Institute held on Tuesday, January 12th, 1926. As you are aware the poultry industry in the province of British Columbia has, during the past few years, developed very rapidly and is probably more attractive in view of the possibility of winter production, so that shipments to the prairie and eastern provinces have been gradually on the increase.
We are, however, faced with what we feel to be very unfair and unjust competition, that from the United States, inasmuch as we are required to pay on eggs exported to that country a duty of 8 cents per dozen but they may be imported into Canada paying thereon only a duty of 3 cents per dozen.
I trust that you will keep the facts herein before you, and should occasion arise endeavour to relieve the situation.
The petition covers what is stated in the letter, and requests some protection for the 14011-24J
industry in the province of British Columbia. Conditions in the dairy and poultry industries are very serious, and no effort has been made to provide relief.
I have been somewhat amused by the attitude of hon. gentlemen to my left. On every occasion they appeal from the standpoint of agriculture. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) the other day applied a term to them which I should not like to apply to the Progressives in this House, for though they may be termed wheat miners, robbers of the soil, or whatever you like to term it, I am sure they have the sympathy of the farmers of our province. The farmers of our province are delighted when they have a good crop, and they sympathize with our Progressive friends when they have a poor one. But we expect from them the same sympathy. We expect them to be interested in other branches of agriculture than the raising of grain. The members of the Progressive party occupy a position of vantage in this House, and are in a position to secure immediately relief for the daily and poultry industries of this Dominion. A few days ago they voted confidence in the government; they are responsible for keeping them in office, and I would suggest that the leader of the Progressive party go to the government and to the Minister of Agriculture and say: "We want you to serve notice immediately of the abrogation of the Australian treaty, which we voted against, and which is ruining the dairy industry of this country." I say also that, though it may be somewhat against their principles, when every man in every district that is engaged in the poultry and dairy industries is demanding the same protection for those industries as similar industries have to the south of the line, the Progressives should be at least fair enough to recommend to the government that they give the Canadian dairy industries this protection.
I feel that I must take a strong stand on the Australian treaty. The people of my constituency demand the immediate abrogation of that treaty, and I think tihis is the feeling in every agricultural district throughout Canada. Some may ask: What about the urban population? I think you will find those people fair when the question is put before them. I do not think they will want to buy butter at three or four cents a pound less when they understand that that would mean the ruination of our dairy industry. The reduction does not apply simply to butter, because, as every one acquainted with the dairy industry knows, the price of milk and all milk products is based on the price of butter fat, and butter
The Address-Mr. Barber

fat in our province is based on the price of butter at Vancouver. If butter in Vancouver drops five or ten cents a pound, the milk which the farmer sells to the creamery immediately drops in price.
I have said that the people of our district are opposed to the continuance of the Australian treaty. They pronounced on that treaty on the 29th day of October last. Gentlemen opposite had in their ranks in the last parliament a representative from the Fraser Valley. He sat on the other side of the House for four years. He is one of our highly respected farmers. He went through the district before the election and although he had been elected by a substantial majority four years before, on October 29, when the sole issue was protection and the Australian treaty, he was turned down by 1,286 votes.

Will the hon.
member tell us what kind of tough grain was selling in the Fraser Valley for over $2 a bushel ?

I could not say; I just
read the item as it appeared in the Province. The grain was purchased in Vancouver. I do not know the exact rates on grain going through Vancouver, but the freight rates question was a very live one in Vancouver, and it drifted out to the constituency which I represent, and during the campaign we all learned something about it. Suppose the export rate on grain from Edmonton or some other point to Vancouver is 21 cents, and that a train composed of 50 cars is shipped from Edmonton to Vancouver, including five cars of grain for local or domestic use. All the cars are landed on the same siding in Vancouver and are hauled by the same engine, but if the export rate on grain is 21 cents, the man buying the grain for domestic use must pay a rate of about 42 cents. That is one of the difficulties we are suffering from, but that of course is a different question from the one I was dealing with tonight.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to farmers on the apposition side of the House and in the Progressive party to endeavour to give some relief to the dairy and poultry industries in this country, which are on the verge of ruination at the present time.

I suppose it is so long, Mr. Speaker, since you have been congratulated on re-election to your high office that further congratulations must be rather refreshing, yet having known during the last four years your eminent fairness and justice and fitness for the position I feel I cannot let this opportunity pass without con-

gratulating you. I also congratulate the mover (Mr. Elliott) and the seconder (Mr. Lacombe) of the Address.
Before entering on what I intend to say on the Address proper, I should like to refer to a few of the arguments that have been used [DOT]by the last two speakers. I can hardly agree with the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gersthaw), who desires an export duty on wheat. The theory is very nice that we should have our wheat ground in Canada, but the theory will not work out. The British millers have their mills, and their money invested in them, and they want wheat to grind, and if Canada refuses to sell them wheat, they will buy it elsewhere.

I would not ask for an
export duty on wheat going to England. Probably I did not make myself clear. I would suggest that the duty should apply only against a country that did not allow our Canadian wheat the advantages in their domestic market that we allow their wheat in our domestic market. I would so draft the regulations 'that wheat exported for domestic use in any other country would not be affected by the duty.

The farmer of the western
prairies looks upon this as a legitimate market which in many cases brings him a better price than he would otherwise get. In the mills of [DOT]the United States, such as the Minneapolis mills with their production of 96,000 barrels a day, they desire a considerable quantity of hard wheat to mix with their soft wheat. Now I admit there is considerable mixing done; in fact I think under one plan where they take our Canadian wheat through in bond it is compulsory for them to mix thirty per cent of their United States wheat with our wheat in order to get the ninety-nine per cent drawback. Under the other plan I believe they simply have to pay the expenses of a government official and the mill is bonded. In that case they pay no duty, but simply the expense of having a government official to look after the mill, and that mill is entirely under his charge while in operation.
I would like to make a remark or two in reply to observations offered by the last speaker, the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber). My hon. friend stated that he was sympathetic to the prairie provinces. He said that in British Columbia they were very much pleased when the prairie provinces enjoyed a good crop. I think I can reciprocate that sentiment, for more reasons than one. We know that when there is a good crop of fruit in British Columbia we are likely to

The Address-Mr. Millar
get fruit cheaper, and they know that when we have a good crop of grain we are going to have more money to pay for British Columbia fruit. My hon. friend was very much exercised about the Australian treaty, as apparently the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) also was yesterday. The fatter hon. member might have asked his desk-mate, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) for information, because When this treaty was up for discussion last year two Conservative members spoke in its favour. We will now see what they said on that occasion. I think you will find that lawyers do not always agree in the advice they give. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. (Manion) said on the occasion referred to:
There is another reason why I feel there is no particular danger to be feared from this agreement. As set out on the orders of the day clause 5 provides-
Clause 5 is somewhat lengthy, but the provision is that the agreement can be terminated by either party upon six months' notice. The hon. member goes on to say:
An agreement which can be cancelled on six months' notice is to my mind not of such a character, in view of the other advantages it gives to this country, as to cause me to vote against it.
The hon. member for Vancouver South, speaking on the same subject-and you will pote the contrast between his advice to the Progressives in this corner of the House last year and the advice given by the hon. member for Fraser Valley to-night-said:
This Australian agreement is a matter of momentous importance to the province of British Columbia in some of its basic industries. The Prime Minister in his remarks has covered a number of the arguments that I had intended to take up. I propose for a few minutes to address my words particularly to my Progressive friends.
And he urged upon them the wisdom of taking a broad conception of the merits and advantages of this agreement and approving of its adoption that night. Further down the same member says:
My hon. friend might have taken my remarks as a compliment to himself, that he at all events, in my estimation, is still open to conviction. The public bodies of Vancouver, such as the Board of Trade, with some 2,000 members, the press of Vancouver-the Province, the Sun and other publications and large business institutions-have energetically and actively supported the idea of an Australian treaty, and until a few days ago I believe most members of the House, particularly in this quarter were equally in favour of the Australian treaty.
Read on.

There is nothing further.
I should! like to refer to a matter which I believe to be of urgent importance. I
am sorry there are only two members of the government present, but I would ask those two ministers, even if they do not pay attention to anything else I may say, to listen to the statement I am about to make. It has nothing to do with the amendment we are considering, but I believe the rules of the House will permit me to bring the matter up. Early in October last, when the threshing of grain was going on in the prairie provinces, there was a very heavy snowstorm. After that for a time there was fine sunny weather, and then snow came again, with the result that millions of bushels of grain were threshed in poor condition. You may say that it was an unwise thing to do, but if that had not been done the snow might have come in such quantities and the weather might have turned so severe that the grain would have had to stand over the winter, with the result that it would have been tom to pieces by stock and prairie chickens and gophers would have fed upon it. A great deal of .destruction would have taken place and the grain would have been very much discoloured. Much of the grain that is in poor condition has been shipped out and there are now upwards of one thousand ears lying in the yards at Fort 'William, while much more is held back in the country. There is no room in the terminal elevators at Fort William to take that grain in and dry it and store it. But something must be done with it. Some cars are worth $2,500, others less; there will certainly be a very heavy loss. Much of that grain instead of coming out in a saleable condition would have to be dug out with shovels in the spring and thrown into the lake. Now that is a very serious matter, and I see only two ways of preventing such a loss. One is to take the grain into the drying elevators, a few cars at a time, dry it and put it back into the cars. The other course is to do what should have been done long ago, reduce the rate over the National Transcontinental to Quebec. If the freight rate from Fort William on the Canadian National railways were lowered to the level of the Crowsnest pass rate, the dry grain in the elevators could be taken to the city of Quebec and put in the elevator there, which has a capacity of 4,000,000 bushels. That would give room to have this damp grain dried and stored in the elevators. These are the only two remedies that I can suggest for meeting the condition in question. I would suggest that the government use its best offices with the railway commission and the railway companies in this Matter. I believe the railways are aware of the danger and perhaps they will see that it is in their best
The Address-Mr. Millar

interest to take such steps as the situation calls for. They will see that if the farmers who have shipped this grain are to sustain this loss it will cripple many of them, indeed many of them will be put out of business. I ask the government to take this matter into consideration. I think every hon. member from the west, whether in Progressive, Conservative or Liberal ranks, should back up some movement. There may be a better remedy-I am not wedded to any particular one-but means should be taken to prevent the loss of the grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will be interested to know that only yesterday a member oif the grain commission brought to my attention the condition prevailing at Fort William. I do not Icnow the condition of the elevator at Quebec to-day, but I do know that about three weeks ago it was almost full. There was room, I believe, for about 400,000 bushels more. I wrote to-day to Mr. E. W. Beatty, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and to Sir Henry Thornton, President of the Canadian National Railways, urging them to take up this matter at once with the grain commissioners and try to work out some plan with a view to doing just exactly what my hon. friend has recommended-that the grain Should be unloaded, dried, and reloaded in the same car. I will let my hon. friend know when I receive a reply.

That is gratifying indeed,
and I thank the minister for his statement.
'With reference to the contents of the Speech from the Throne, I will pass very lightly over the Hudson Bay railway, not because it is not desired in my constituency-we are all most anxious to have it-but because the matter has been pretty fully discussed. We must compete in the markets of the world with our cattle and our grain. Since Port Nelson is approximately one thousand miles nearer to the centre of the grain fields than Montreal, and since Port Nelson and Montreal are practically equidistant from Liverpool, Port Nelson has a great advantage over Montreal. Because mark you, although we have some water between Fort William and Montreal, the route is a circuitous one, and much of it, is canal, and almost as expensive as the railway; so that it costs just about the same to take the grain from Fort William to Montreal over the water and rail rowte as it would cost to take the grain from Armstrong, immediately north of Fort William on the Canadian National,
[Mr. Millar.}
to the city of Quebec. The cost would be just about the same if it were under the Crowsnest agreement rate, but unfortunately instead of 11| cents the rate is about 21 cents. Why that is I do not know. The question has been asked many times in the House, who is responsible for it? The railway was built at a cost of $170,000,000, and anyone reading the argument presented when the 10 p.m. building of the railway was being discussed will see that the central thought in the minds of all was that it should be constructed of such a standard and grade that it would be able to compete for the transport of our Canadian grain, keep it in Canadian channels and take it to Quebec.
After the railway was completed, what was done? I understand the rate at one time was six cents a bushel from Armstrong to the city of Quebec, and I believe Mr. Symington, in presenting his case before a committee of this parliament one or two years ago, was able to prove that the railways at that time, at the rate of six cents a bushel, made a profit. I am not sure of that and I am open to correction. Then I believe it jumped to 24 cents a bushel, and is now back to about 21 cents-a most absurd situation, after building a railway at that expense. We have an elevator at Quebec with a capacity of four million bushels, yet the rails are rusting and the ties rotting over part of the line. Surely that should be remedied. I am glad there was a suggestion in the Speech from the Throne that the reason our grain goes through American channels would be investigated, in which case this other question would have to receive consideration. But I am inclined to think that both matters could be better dealt with, especially the former, by a committee of this House than by the railway commission.
In reference to the question of the return to the western provinces of their natural resources, I am glad to see that Alberta is going to get back its natural resources-something it should have had long ago.
Rural credits is a matter of vital importance, and I look upon this as one of the most important measures proposed to this House. One of the great burdens of the western farmer is 'that he has to pay an interest rate of eight, t< n and twelve per cent. And because he is paying that rate of interest he becomes financially enbarrassed and his credit is impaired. Instead of becoming wealthier he becomes poorer, and just as soon as he gets a little poorer and his credit is impaired, the banks refuse him credit-sometimes absolutely refuse him any credit. In regard to the

The Address-Mr. Millar
banks, white I wish to be fair toward them,
I must say that some instances have come to my notice in which I thought they were very unfair and very inconsiderate.
I will mention an isolated case. A farmer in my constituency borrowed last year from the bank in his town three small sums, amounting to $260, on three notes. The notes did not fall due till October or November, but on the first of July he had some money coming in from wheat on what we call the participation certificates, that is, the second or third payment from the pool. The bank, without his consent, and he claims without any arrangement or agreement oin his part, deliberately kept his money and cancelled the notes, notwithstanding the fact that he had paid interest up to November on the money he borrowed. I thought it was rather unfair. However, the trouble is not so much with the banks, because generally the amount a farmer is able to borrow from the banks is a very small sum,. What he borrows from the loan companies is four, five or six times as much. In some cases during the last three years when the farmer was unable to meet his mortgage when it matured, the rate was increased one per cent, so that what he could not pay at eight per cent, they thought, "Well, we will see if he can pay nine per cent." Or if he could not pay nine per cent, "we will see if he can pay ten per cent." Some system of rural credits should be introduced. I agree with hon. members who have stated! that this matter must be handled very carefully. I sometimes agree with the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) but I did not quite agree with him when he was speaking in Regina and referred to me in the rather endearing term of wolf. I agree with him when he says that he does not approve of direct loans being made to the farmers by the government.
I did not catch the remark the hon. member made with reference to myself.

I was informed that when
the right hon. gentleman was speaking in Regina he referred to me by the endearing term of "wolf."

I may have referred to
my hon. friend as a grit, but I never Called him a wolf.
Misquoted.
I do not think my hon. friend can get the quotation either.

Another matter of considerable importance is, why does our Canadian grain go so largely through American channels? This is a matter that is not well understood by a great many of our people. The reason I believe is almost entirely economic. I notice that some blame the Canadian National management, others the Canadian Pacific, and some have complained of both, because their grain is not going through Canadian ports. I think the railways have very little to do in deciding its course. A shipper decides by which route his grain is going to reach its ultimate destination at the cheapest possible rate, and that settles the matter. Many great liners coming to the city of New York are anxious to have our grain as ballast and will therefore carry it very cheaply. More come there than to Montreal and, while at the moment I am speaking only from memory, although the distance from New York to Liverpool is 500 miles further than from Montreal to Liverpool, this causes our grain to be carried from New York at about one and one-half cents a bushel less than from Montreal. That is a handicap which it is hard to overcome. On the other hand the western farmer does not look upon it as a handicap. He believes he gets his grain carried to the ultimate market at a lower price because those great liners are carrying it more cheaply. Some have asked: If the United States route is the cheaper, how is it that so much United States grain goes through Canadian ports? I am not sure that I can give a full explanation, but I believe one factor is this:	In the early part of the season,
when United States grain, particularly corn, is moving to the waterfront, United States boats are very busy carrying ore. They find that trade more lucrative and they feel reluctant to leave the ore business for the grain. They are not anxious at that time to carry grain. On the other hand, Canadian boats, because of the coastal regulations, cannot carry United States grain from one United States port to another, but they can carry it to a Canadian port. At that season of the year, before our grain has started to move, one can readily understand that our Canadian boats are likely, if not to be entirely idle, to have a very slack season, and rather than be idle, they are ready to carry United States grain to a Canadian port at a reasonable rate. I believe that is one of the most important factors in deciding the route of United States grain, and it goes through Canadian channels for that reason. Moreover, at that season more space is available at Mont-
The Address-Mr. Millar

ton of tomatoes annually. He is an expert at preparing his produce for the shows. He goes to Regina every year. This year he won sixty-eight prizes, forty of them firsts. He goes down into the United States to the dry farming fairs, and is always a prize-winner. He is a real gardener. His Excellency the Governor General seldom comes to Indian Head without visiting that man's garden. This fall he placed in a store window, a small space about seven or eight feet square, probably the finest exhibit of vegetables that has ever been seen in western Canada. I spoke to him about it and said that it would be interesting and instructive if that exhibit could be displayed in the city of Ottawa just when the members are here. "Now," he replied, "I will present that exhibit as a free gift." I wrote to the Canadian National Railway and all I asked was that they give free transportation and perhaps display the exhibit in their window on Sparks street. It was all prepared by an expert, ready to be sent down. I was rather disappointed when after five or six weeks I was told that the National Railway people were so lacking in window space that they could hardly do what I had requested. I think I will make the same offer to the Canadian Pacific Railway if I can next year, and then I may be able to show what can be done in western Canada along horticultural lines.	[DOT]
Hon. members will probably be surprised to leam that on the experimental farm at Indian Head, there is not a greenhouse worthy the name. The gardener I speak of starts his tomatoes in a greenhouse, and the plants are a good size and ready to transplant when the frost is over. As I said, he raises each year more than a ton of ripe tomatoes; other vegetables in proportion. For instance, he had on display a box of twenty onions weighing 45 pounds. It was marvellous. Similar results can be obtained all over the prairie provinces. It seems to me that some money might well be expended by the government to build a greenhouse at Indian Head and put it in charge of a good staff in the interests of horticulture, so that what can be done in the prairie provinces in the growing of fruits and vegetables may be demonstrated. I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) will ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for the necessary expenditure for this purpose. If this woii'k is undertaken I fully expect the time will come when we will not have to buy so much fruit from the Fraser valley.

There is a matter which I have dealt with before and which I would like to mention again. Those who live in the west, and especially those who are farming, know what an enormous expense it is to the farmer to have to pay the present prices for repairs for machinery. This fall a neighbour told me of an experience he had. He wanted to thresh but he had broken a concave, so he went to Regina to get a new one. It cost a considerable sum, and it was very brittle; when he tapped it with a hammer in putting it in place it fell to pieces, and the only way he could get his threshing done was to engage a blacksmith to make a new concave. The cost of these repairs seems far higher than it should be. Then there is the cost of repairs for cars. I think if a committee were appointed to take up the work of standardization of parts and the cost of repairs we would get somewhere.
I do not like to criticize the discussion which has taken place during the past few days. I can see that when wrong things are done in election time there is some benefit in bringing them to the light of day, but I fancy there has been rather too much of this in the course of this debate. It brings to my mind a story which I heard once about a court case. There were of course, two lawyers and a judge, and immediately the case started the two lawyers got into a heated altercation. One called the other a liar, and the other retorted with an equally offensive name. The judge said, "Now, gentlemen, you are each identified; proceed with the case." I -think I may say to both sides of the House that you are now identified, and I think we might proceed with business. I must say that I agree largely with both. There is a lot of important business which should be put through. The people of Canada are not particularly anxious about what Patenaude or some other man said, they want some redress for their grievances, some legislation which will be effective and which will enable them to make good. That is what the people of Canada want. I quite understand that when one man breaks out with a tirade and makes certain charges, replies are likely to be made. If you will permit me another story-I should not tell so many, but one more will do no harm-the remarks of the hon. member for Kent, NH. (Mr. Doueet) and what followed reminded me of something I saw at the theatre the other night. A young man was running after a pet dog, and was particularly anxious to catch it. Every time he got close enough to reach for it however, the dog was not there. At

The Address-Mr. Millar
last the dog -ran in through a little square hole in a fence. The young man reached his arm in and pulled out a dog, but it turned out to be a bulldog. The -point is, he got what he did not expect to get.
I would like to touch briefly on the amendment. As I understand it, it certainly includes protection, and I think there is a great deal too much being said with regard to what are alleged to be the beneficial effects of protection on eggs, butter, cheese and other farm products. Mark this, that while there may be some exceptions, in the main you cannot by making provision for freer imports injure any tracte which is on an export basis. Something was read in this House the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) to the effect that on a certain day eggs had come to Vancouver from Australia or New Zealand and cut the price three -cents. I wondered if the price which was cut had been fixed by the cold storage plants, after cornering the eggs and raising the price above the export values. I would remind you that in the winter time, when eggs are not very plentiful, a great many people selling eggs are too far from the seaboard to be affected by the competition, be-jause they have a little market in their own community. Take the matter of butter, eggs, cheese, etc. I need not give the figures, since they were, given the other cliay, but we are exporting enormous quantities, and we cannot be seriously affected by such competition. If other countries could ruin our prices for eggs and other things, why cannot Australia ruin our price for wheat? Simply because, if Australia brought 50,000,000 bushels of wheat into Canada, the Canadian wheat so displaced would simply fill up the space left in the British market. Do not forget that eggs in Australia, butter in New Zealand, and all these other commodities are parts of the visible supply. They are in the world, and if we do not compete with them here we will compete with them somewhere else. I will admit that there are times when the prices of some of these commodities rise a little above export value, and then there is created an opportunity for foreign products to come in and cut the price. There may be a few individuals who will be injured in a case of that kind, but only a very, very small number. When the cold storage plants have cornered the market and raised the price above the export basis, it may be that foreign eggs will come in and compel them to -bring that price down. Do not forget that somebody is benefited in such a case; do not forget that thousands
are buying eggs and are being held up by the cold storage plants, which reap the benefit.
I think I have said enough about our wheat. The price of wheat is higher in the United States than in Canada and always will be, -because of the greater population and the greater demand. Then I would like to offer one word in reply to a criticism made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meigben). There have been times when he has made too sweeping denunciations, and one of those times was in connection with the Grain Inquiry Commission. During the past twenty or twenty-five years I think we have had three grain inquiries. We find that since we have had these inquiries our grain trade, while it has its evils, is clean in comparison with some other industries. It is clean as compared with the fruit industry, for example. Why is that? Largely because of these inquiries. The information is taken publicly; it is published in the papers; the farmers come to the various sittings, give evidence and listen to others giving evidence. They study the evidence and reports, and there is very little that can take place in the grain trade which the farmer will not find out. In an elevator in Vancouver a spout was operated which, to my mind, was built for the purpose of-well, I think I must use the word-stealing. The spout was built in this way: there is a conveyor or leg which carries the grain up, and a spout which brings it down again to the weigher. Underneath this spout was a hole to which was attached another spout, and by an adjustment of the slides the grain could be taken to the cleaner instead of to the weigher. The grain inquiry commission investigated the matter and the blame was placed by the harbour commission on the grain board. It was proved that the grain board were not responsible. The blame was then placed on the chief weighmaster, but he showed that he was not responsible and that he was greatly alarmed when he heard of it. To make a long story short it was found that a great many men had been taken on as employees in that elevator who had formerly been employed at Fort William. I am afraid the harbour commission were not such grain experts as harbour commissioners should be. There was a firm at Fort William which had operated the only other elevator .in Canada with this peculiar spout. That was discovered, and as we dug deeper and deeper, we became more and more suspicious, and the result, as told to me by one of the harbour commissioners, was this: "After you fellows left there", he said, "I went down and fired every
The Address-Mr. Millar

one of those men." They made a general cleanup.
The Grain Inquiry Commission went through the country, and found evils, small ones 'mostly. In one case they found that the beams of the scales had been filed. An inspector, according to sworn evidence, had said: "You get me a file and I will show you how our fellows get a little wheat," and he filed the shoulder of the beam so that the weight in balancing the scale need not be at zero, but about one-eighth of an inch, I think it was, nearer to the shoulder of the beam: and by experimenting they found that that gave them about sixty pounds to the load. That is only one irregularity of dozens, yes scores, that were discovered. For instance, they discovered the mixing of poor wheat with the good. The whole trade was investigated from one end to the other, and last session the Grain Act was revised by a committee of experts. The chief inspector, the members of the grain commission, the secretary of the Grain Exchange, and several members on this side of the House and in other parts of the House who understood the grain trade pretty well, spent weeks diligently revising the Grain Act, and I believe the reason our grain trade is comparatively clean to-day is because of just such work. It is difficult to lay your finger on any one thing you can consider a big reform. There were a few,-not very many, but taken altogether a great improvement was made. The right hon. leader of the opposition has said that the grain inquiry if everything be included cost $500,000. The commission itself did not cost half that much, but even if it did cost that much, when you divide that expense over the grain produced in only one season, the amount is next to nothing; it is almost lost sight of; and when you consider the benefits that will be reaped by those growing grain for the next ten years perhaps, the expense is not to be mentioned; it is not worth considering.
It is true that there were three important clauses that we were unable to get through the committee. Why? Because, I am sorry to say, members on both sides of the House who knew as little about the grain trade as I know about growing tobacco came to the committee and voted us down again andl again when we were almost unanimous on what we wanted. Now that is not wise; it is not fair. I think it would be equally ridiculous if I and my fellow-members, who know nothing about growing tobacco, were deliberately to vote down a certain reform that the tobacco growers of Quebec and Ontario united in asking for.

The Speech from the Throne contains very much that I want, and want h * lly, and that the people of my constituency want. I have noticed a generous spirit amongst Quebec members towards the west.
Hear, hear.

Do not say "hear, hear" too soon. I noticed an item in the paper recently that made me sit up and take notice. It intimated that the harbour board of Montreal would ask for perhaps ten or twenty million dollars this year. It may be that the harbour board of Montreal requires to make further improvements, but, mark youf the parts of Canada that have not been getting their just share in the past are the Maritime provinces, the western prairie provinces, and two years ago I would have said the fruit-growers of British Columbia. Now I think it would be wise if the people of Ontario and Quebec would1 just have patience for another year until we can build up those parts of Canada that are in distress. Do not say to us, " we will take say ten million dollars to be spent in the central provinces, and we will give you four or five millions for the west." We are not exactly in distress in the western provinces. There is optimism and a considerably better feeling there; we are not hopeless by any means. Give us cheaper money, not easier money, and a few other things, and we will make good. The west is coming back, and coming back fast, but give us a few of the things we really need and do not take too much for Ontario and1 Quebec. Let the people down here have patience for a year. It is not forgotten by this House that Toronto got $7,500,000 for its viaduct, Montreal $5,000,000 for a new bridge, and Quebec $5,000,000 for harbour improvements last session. Money has been spent fairly freely in these two central provinces, and I think there will be a very much better feeling if you will have a little further patience in Ontario and Quebec and first build up the other parts of the country, and try to solve the problem of the Maritime provinces.
There is only one thing I have to say about the Maritimes that may perhaps give offence, but my opinion is that when the government built an elevator at Halifax they might as well have thrown the money into the sea. In my humble judgment-I may be wrong; I hope I am-Halifax can never be made a grain port. If one million dollars had been spent to help those provinces which I am convinced need help, I would have been very glad indeed to support that expenditure. But I say that that problem down by the

Alberta Coal
sea should be solved, and if something practical can be done to put the Maritime provinces on their feet it will be for the benefit, not only of (those provinces, but of the Dominion as a whole, for we want a united Canada. I think perhaps my thoughts are better expressed in this little pamphlet than I can express them myself, so 1 will close with the following quotation, and leave you to guess the source until I get through:
Bear in mind that all classes in our Dominion are just as much affected by inequitable transportation costs as are the grain producers of Western Canada. Never overlook what the fact is, that the source of all wealth is original Mother Earth. That is why the railroad owner, the railroad worker, the manufacturers and their employees, banks and their staffs can only be assured of conserving their own property and their own positions when the grain grower and the cattle breeder are assured of a fair living wage for their labour. In a word, the future success of our country depends upon the prosperity of our farm life.
The grain grower is the foundation for a broad and high pyramid of population; he is the ultimate consumer of what most of the rest of our people produce.
I would draw the attention of the leader of the opposition particularly to this sentence which follows:
If we fill our country with happy and contented grain growers and cattle breeders, who are assured of a fair living wage, every man in a factory, every man in a shop, every man in a railway, every man in an office will be in a vastly better and safer position.
Who do you suppose wrote that? The hon. *member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers).
